facts: The main server runs Proxmox and hosts most of the virtual machines.
The NAS uses ZFS with two mirrored drives and is named bunker.

Backups run nightly at 2 a.m. to the NAS, and a weekly copy goes to an offsite cloud bucket. Retention is thirty daily snapshots and twelve monthly ones. Restore tests happen every quarter on a spare VM. A backup does not count until a restore has been tested.
DNS for the home network runs on a Raspberry Pi with Pi-hole.
Home services are reachable only over the VPN; the router opens no ports.

Every service runs in a container with a fixed version tag, and the latest tag is never used. Updates are applied on the first Sunday of each month after a snapshot. Services that break after an update are rolled back immediately, and the failed version is noted in the changelog. Container images are pulled from the private registry only.
Certificates are issued automatically and renew every sixty days.
Nadia lives in the other apartment and helps with the printer when it breaks.

Monitoring uses Grafana dashboards fed by a metrics collector on each host. Alerts go to a phone notification and to a chat channel, but only for failures that last more than ten minutes. Disk usage above 85 percent triggers a warning, and above 95 percent triggers a page. Dashboards are reviewed on the first weekend of each month.
Theo helps with network setup, and he is on call only on weekends.
Power for the server rack goes through a battery backup that lasts about twenty minutes.
The server room is the cupboard under the stairs, which stays below 27 degrees.

Public domains point to the home IP through a dynamic DNS record that updates every fifteen minutes. If the IP changes, the old record stays cached for an hour. Certificates for public domains are issued through the DNS challenge. Never publish internal hostnames in public DNS.
Passwords are kept in a self-hosted password manager, never in config files.
The media server is a mini PC in the living room, streaming to the TV.

New devices join the home network on the IoT VLAN, which cannot reach the main network. Smart plugs and cameras go there by default. Guest devices use a separate Wi-Fi network with a time limit. Anything that needs access to the NAS must be added by hand to the firewall rules.
The server's electricity costs are split evenly between me and Nadia.

The hardware inventory lives in a spreadsheet with serial numbers, warranty dates, and purchase prices. Drives older than five years are replaced preemptively. Failed drives are wiped before disposal, and the NAS keeps a spare disk on the shelf. Warranty claims go through the vendor portal.
New VMs need a description, owner tag, and backup policy before going live.
I update the DNS blocklists once a month, after the Pi's weekly report.

The lab rule is that I do not experiment on the main server during working hours; I use the test VM instead. Changes to the router are scheduled for Saturday mornings. Before any experiment, I write a rollback plan in the notes. If an experiment causes an outage, I post in the household chat within fifteen minutes.
Guest Wi-Fi access details are updated every quarter and posted on the fridge whiteboard.
Old laptops are used as spare test machines and are wiped every six months.

Every service has a documented owner, and the owner decides when it is retired. Retired services are archived for ninety days before deletion. Shutdowns are announced in the household chat one week in advance. Anyone who depends on a service must export their data first.
